1:
The interval is the first thing weighed. Robertson allows the sixth day itself but thinks a week likelier, since Luke says about eight; Ellicott takes Luke's phrase for the loose reckoning that called some six-and-thirty hours three days. Chrysostom asks why Jesus waited and gives two reasons: that the other disciples might not be touched with jealousy, and that those going up might be kindled with more desire meanwhile. Origen takes the six days mystically: in six days the whole visible world was made, so a man above the things of this world may climb the mountain and see the glory of the Word. Ellicott notes that the same three keep the place they held at the raising of the ruler's daughter; Henry, that the scene was meant for an earnest of the kingdom Christ had just spoken of.

What changed is carefully defined. Barnes says the word means a change of appearance and not of substance; Gill, that neither the substance of the body nor its shape was altered, only that it received a more glorious form. Robertson identifies the word as the one behind the metamorphoses of the poets, touching the form and not the fashion, which is the outward accident. Clarke and Wesley make it a disclosure: the fullness of the Godhead that dwelt bodily in Christ shone out through the human nature, the indwelling Deity darting its rays through the veil of the flesh, so that he no longer bore the form of a servant. Leo calls the lesson a great mystery, better understood if we attend to what is narrated just before it.

The two who appear raise a question of fact. Calvin asks whether they were really present or only shown in vision, as the prophets often saw absent things, and judges it more probable they were actually brought there. Ellicott thinks the recognition intuitive, an illumination belonging to the state they had been raised to. Barnes explains why these two, Moses having given the law whose types were now fulfilled; Clarke presses the bodies, Elijah coming in the body he was translated in and Moses probably raised as a pledge of the resurrection.

Peter is handled gently, but not spared. Robertson quotes Bruce, that Peter is to the front and not greatly to his credit, and recalls Luke's note that he did not know what he said, the three being heavy with sleep; Gill and Lightfoot make it a thing of the night, the disciples waking to it. Calvin finds in the offer a fear that the sight would vanish when the visitors left, and does not wonder Peter was so captivated. Wesley calls the words rapturous surprise and notices the arithmetic, three tents and not six, because the apostles meant to stay with their Master.

The cloud corrects the mistake. Clarke argues that a bright cloud can cast no shade, so the verb should be rendered surrounded rather than overshadowed; Barnes agrees it means diffused over them and not darkening them. Chrysostom contrasts Sinai, where the darkness was meant to terrify, with this brightness, whose purpose was to teach, and notes that neither Moses nor Elijah speaks but the Father. Robertson marks the difference from the baptism, where the same words were addressed to Jesus and are here spoken to the disciples about him; Wesley reduces the command to its point, that they hear him as superior even to Moses and the prophets.

The ending is read as the lesson in miniature. Calvin says the Law and the Prophets had a temporary glory so that Christ alone might remain in view, and a man who would use Moses rightly must not stop with him but be led by his hand to Christ; Ellicott adds that it was not good for frail men to tarry in that Presence, and a relief to see Jesus only.
9:
The order of silence is explained from several directions. Barnes says the vision was meant to confirm these three that he was the Messiah, so while he remained with them there was no need to report it, though after the crucifixion they would need the evidence. Ellicott points out that the prohibition covered the other apostles too, who at their lower stage of growth would have either distrusted the report at second hand or perverted it. Wesley gives both halves of the danger, that the rest would be grieved at not being admitted and outsiders either enraged or, when the sufferings came, incredulous. Clarke adds a political reason, that a matter certain to irritate the Jewish rulers was better kept quiet. Calvin says plainly that the disciples themselves would not have believed it without the more striking proof of the resurrection, and Robertson notes from Mark that they were puzzled even by the word about rising again.

The question they raise is about the scribes rather than the vision. Chrysostom observes that the disciples learned the coming of Elijah not from the Scriptures but from the scribes, whose teaching had become current among the ignorant multitude, as their teaching about Christ had. Ellicott thinks the question came from the three alone, brooding over the appearance and still more the disappearance of Elijah; Clarke notes that some manuscripts read simply the disciples, meaning those who had been on the mount. Robertson puts the difficulty exactly: they had just seen Elijah, but the Messiah had come before him, and the scribes had Malachi on their side. Calvin traces the confusion further back, since no sooner is the resurrection mentioned than they imagine the reign of Christ already begun. Wesley hears in the question an objection to the silence just imposed, that if the coming is not to be told, they might rather tell every man.

The answer is granted first and then qualified, and the commentators disagree about how far. Barnes says the scribes' doctrine was true and Jesus does not deny it, since he immediately adds that Elijah has come. Ellicott finds the words deliberately enigmatic, admitting two very different interpretations, since taken literally many in earlier and later times have read them of an Elijah still to come. Calvin explains the root of the error, that John was to resemble Elijah in restoring a fallen Church and Malachi had given him that name, which the scribes interpreted rashly. Lightfoot supplies what the rabbis expected of the restorer, that he purify the doubtful births and bring back the pot of manna, the vial of holy oil and the vial of water.

Two of the fathers pull the verse in other directions. Origen uses it to refuse the doctrine of transmigration outright: that Elijah is already come is not to be understood of the soul of Elijah, lest we fall into metempsychosis, which is foreign to the truth of the Church's doctrine, but as the angel foretold, of one who came in the spirit and power of Elijah. Augustine takes the restoring of all things forward instead, of those whom the persecution of Antichrist shall have overthrown, as Christ himself restores by his death.

The identification is then made plain. Robertson says Jesus identifies John with the promise in Malachi while not making him the Elijah in person that John denied being; Wesley gives the same distinction in the Baptist's own words, that he was not Elijah the Tishbite come again but the man of whom the prophecy spoke under that name. Gill and Clarke note that it was the account of the ill usage which made it clear; Ellicott finds the closing verse suggestive twice over, for the conclusion the disciples rested in and for the frankness with which they owned how slowly they passed from the literalism of the scribes. Robertson simply calls it plain enough even for them.
14:
The descent from the mountain is felt as a contrast. Origen makes it a rebuke of the request just refused, since Peter had preferred his own benefit in wishing to stay, but charity seeks not her own and Jesus went down. Ellicott notes from Luke that this was the next day, the night having been spent on the mount. Henry sets the scene as a melancholy case brought to Christ the moment he came down from the glory above.

The boy's disorder is described medically and then theologically. Robertson glosses the word as moonstruck, the symptoms of epilepsy being supposed to worsen with the changes of the moon; Clarke says the same and insists the lunacy was still occasioned by a demon; Wesley reconciles the two, that the word is used with propriety though the case was preternatural, since an evil spirit would take advantage of the moon's influence on brain and nerves. Chrysostom draws out what the father's words imply about providence, that a demon who threw the boy into fire and water would have killed him outright had God not restrained him; Augustine reads the two elements morally, the fire of anger that aims upward and the water of fleshly lust.

The rebuke that follows is aimed variously. Lightfoot says its edge is levelled especially at the scribes, though the disciples are not untouched; Calvin agrees that though the words appear addressed to the father they are meant for the scribes, the reproof not being for the ignorant and weak. Ellicott divides it between scribes and disciples, both wanting the faith that utters itself in prayer; Barnes and Robertson explain the word rendered perverse as twisted or turned out of its proper direction; Origen makes the perversity a thing contrary to nature that enters stealthily and distorts.

The failure of the nine is what the disciples themselves ask about. Chrysostom says they had received power over unclean spirits and feared they had forfeited the grace once given. Ellicott notes the question came from those left below, who still did not see the reason. Clarke puts it sharply, that they were confounded at their want of success but not at their want of faith, which caused it; Calvin, that they wondered at a power taken away which they had lost by their own fault. Gill places the conversation in a house, apart from the crowd.

The mustard seed is read four ways. Robertson calls little faith a good rendering and says theirs was less than a grain of mustard seed. Ellicott prefers the harder reading of unbelief and finds the variant a specimen of the tendency to tone down the severity of our Lord's words. Barnes takes the seed for the smallest of seeds, so that the feeblest genuine faith would serve. Origen turns the figure round: faith is like the mustard seed because it is looked on with contempt and shows as something poor and mean, yet falling on a good heart it becomes a great tree. Gregory presses the seed further, that it gives out its qualities only when bruised, so persecution rouses in a holy man what had seemed weak into the heat of virtue. Augustine reads the mountain as earthly pride, which disciples working miracles are warned to remove.

The last verse turns on what kind is meant. Barnes, Gill and Calvin take it of this kind of devils, Calvin adding that Christ was reproving negligence by showing that no ordinary faith was required; Ellicott finds in it degrees in the intensity of evil amounting to a generic difference. Clarke reports that some refer the phrase instead to the faith, which does not exert itself but by prayer and fasting, and rejects that reading. Wesley calls the verse a testimony to the efficacy of fasting added to fervent prayer, noting that other kinds the apostles had cast out without it.
22:
This is the third warning of the passion, and Gill notes it was given as they moved on toward Judea and the passover, so that the disciples might be prepared for the death and not terrified by it. Ellicott prefers as they went to and fro to while they abode in Galilee, the journeying being unconnected with the work of the ministry; Mark says he would not that any man should know of their presence, and Luke adds the charge that these sayings sink down into your ears. The substance was what they had heard before, but Ellicott finds that the repetition gave it new force, showing it was not a mere foreboding of disaster that would pass away with the mood of sadness in which it might seem to have begun.

Origen denies that the Lord is simply repeating himself. What is new is the word betrayed, for he had not before said that he must be delivered into the hands of men. Origen then holds both agencies at once, that the Son was delivered up by the Father according to Romans 8:32 while different powers gave him into the hands of men. Clarke presses the first side alone, following Grotius and Wakefield that the verb should be rendered delivered up rather than betrayed and the agency referred to God, with Acts 4:27-28 for warrant. Barnes takes the second, that to betray is to deliver up in a treacherous manner, and that this was done by Judas, who made use of the confidence reposed in him.

Henry dwells on the phrase into the hands of men - men to whom he was allied by nature and from whom he might have expected pity, men he had undertaken to save and from whom he might have expected gratitude, and these are his persecutors and murderers. Nothing less than his blood would satisfy their rage, and nothing less would answer his own undertaking, since without blood there is no remission. Henry notes that whenever he spoke of his death he gave a hint of the resurrection, the joy set before him for which he endured the cross and despised the shame.

Calvin explains why the warning had to be repeated: the nearer the death approached the more often Christ spoke of it, lest the spectacle give a violent shock to their faith. They had heard it several times and were alarmed as if nothing of it had ever reached their ears, so great is the influence of preconceived opinion, which brings darkness over the mind in the midst of the clearest light. They had imagined a kingdom prosperous and delightful and universally welcomed, and never thought it possible that the rulers of the church would oppose him. Calvin draws the rule that when the death of Christ is mentioned we ought always to take into view at once the whole of the three days. Chrysostom makes a narrower version of the same point, that this is no long time to speak of continuing in death.

The closing note divides the commentators. Robertson takes their exceeding sorrow as a sign that they at last understood he was talking about his death and resurrection. Ellicott reads it the other way from Mark and Luke, who say they understood not the saying and were afraid to ask him; their sorrow was vague and dim, and they shrank from what might make it more definite. Barnes offers three reasons for the failure: their attachment to him, their unwillingness to believe it, and their expectation of a distinguished Prince who would restore the kingdom to Israel, so that a death at his enemies' hands frustrated everything they looked for.
24:
The didrachma is not Caesar's money. Clarke says it was not a tax to the Roman government but the half shekel of Exodus 30:13 for the support of the temple; Barnes and Wesley agree it was voluntary rather than exacted, Wesley calling it a thing which custom rather than any law had established. Lightfoot supports the identification from Josephus and from the Talmudists, who speak of those that collect the shekels where Matthew has those that receive the didrachma. Robertson adds that the tax fell due in the month Adar and was now nearly six months overdue. Calvin dissents: he takes it for the sacred tax that the kings of Asia and then the Romans appropriated, so that the Jews paid to profane tyrants what they had formerly paid to God alone.

They ask Peter rather than Jesus. Chrysostom explains it from the origin of the tax in the redemption of the firstborn, so that they came to the firstborn son through the first among the disciples. Ellicott thinks their question implies they half suspected the Prophet of Nazareth would disclaim payment. Gill and Henry both note that Christ did not stay away to avoid the demand but came to Capernaum, where Peter kept the house and was presumed to know his Master's mind;

The question of the sons is read at two depths. Barnes takes it plainly: kings do not tax their own sons, the money is for the service of the temple, and the Son of God for whom it is gathered cannot lawfully be required to pay it. Clarke extends the exemption to the disciples, as ministering priests were. Robertson calls them logically free but practically not. Ellicott argues the range is wider, since on the narrow reading the Israelites who paid would be aliens rather than sons; he makes it a judgment against the Pharisees, who had lately carried in the Sanhedrin the point that the temple rate be compulsory. Augustine puts it shortest, that if children are free in every kingdom, much more are they free who are children of that kingdom under which all the kingdoms of the earth lie. Origen turns the terms over: the sons of the kings of the earth are not the free ones, since whoever sins is the servant of sin, and the free are those who abide in the word.

Christ pays regardless. Henry draws the rule that prudence and humility teach us to recede from our right rather than give offence by insisting on it, though we must never decline a duty for that reason. Gill applies it to giving no offence to Jew or Gentile or the church of God, even at our own disadvantage. Gregory sets the limit: we must cast about how to avoid scandalising our neighbours as far as we may without sin, but if offence is taken from truth, it is better that offence should come than that truth be forsaken.

The stater divides the commentators over what kind of wonder it was. Clarke lays out the alternatives, that the coin was already in the fish, or that the fish was impelled to fetch it, or that it was created for the purpose, any of which shows wisdom or power. Barnes prefers foreknowledge to creation. Robertson also calls it a miracle of foreknowledge, and rejects the older rationalist readings as a nervous anxiety to relieve the Gospel of the miraculous. Calvin says the point was to prove a dominion wider than any earthly king's, the sea itself paying him tribute. Ellicott alone hesitates: there is no record that the miracle was wrought, the narrative ending without the words we expect, and the wonder stands alone in its kind. Henry, less troubled, notes that the coin was exactly enough for two and no more, Christ making the fish his cash keeper and teaching us not to covet superfluities.
